Threads per transform

Source: R/workers.R
fft_workers.Rd

fft_workers() gets or sets the number of threads a transform uses when its workers argument is NULL. with_fft_workers() sets it while code runs and local_fft_workers() until the calling function returns, in the style of the withr package; both restore the old value. Together they are SciPy's get_workers() and set_workers().

Usage

fft_workers(n = NULL)

with_fft_workers(n, code)

local_fft_workers(n, .local_envir = parent.frame())

Arguments

n

A non-zero whole number. NULL (in fft_workers()) only reads the current value.

code

Code to run with n threads.

.local_envir

The environment whose exit restores the old value.

Value

fft_workers() returns the current value when n is NULL, and otherwise the previous value, invisibly. with_fft_workers() returns the value of code; local_fft_workers() returns the previous value, invisibly.

Details

A positive value asks for that many threads; a negative one counts back from the number of available cores, so -1 means all of them. Requests are capped at the available cores, and at 2 when _R_CHECK_LIMIT_CORES_ is set (as during R CMD check). The initial value is 1, as in SciPy.

Threads help when a transform has many independent lines (the columns of a matrix, a multi-dimensional array) and at least 32 768 elements; a single 1-D real transform always runs on one thread. Results agree to rounding whatever the number of threads, and are bit-identical on builds without fused multiply-add, such as CRAN's x86-64 binaries.

Examples

fft_workers()
#> [1] 1
with_fft_workers(2, fft_c2c(matrix(rnorm(1e4), 100), axes = 1))
